final_proof:
To prove that $\mathcal{A}_n$ is a discrete set of subsets for any $n \in \mathbb{N}_{> 0}$, we must show that for every point $p \in X$, there exists a "neighborhood" of $p$ that intersects at most one element of $\mathcal{A}_n$. In the topology generated by the uniform-like entourages $V_k$, the set $V_k(p) = \{z \in X : (p, z) \in V_k\}$ is a neighborhood of $p$. We will demonstrate that for any $p \in X$, the neighborhood $V_{n+2}(p)$ intersects at most one set in $\mathcal{A}_n$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}_{> 0}$ be given. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there exists a point $p \in X$ such that $V_{n+2}(p)$ intersects two distinct sets in $\mathcal{A}_n$. Let these sets be $A_n(x)$ and $A_n(y)$ for some $x, y \in X$ with $x \neq y$. 

Since $\preccurlyeq$ is a well-ordering on $X$, it is a total ordering. Thus, without loss of generality, we may assume that $y \prec x$.

Because $V_{n+2}(p)$ intersects both sets, we can choose elements:
$u \in V_{n+2}(p) \cap A_n(x)$
$v \in V_{n+2}(p) \cap A_n(y)$

From $u \in V_{n+2}(p)$, we have $(p, u) \in V_{n+2}$. Since $V_{n+2}$ is symmetric, this implies $(u, p) \in V_{n+2}$. 
From $v \in V_{n+2}(p)$, we have $(p, v) \in V_{n+2}$.
By the definition of composite relation, since $(u, p) \in V_{n+2}$ and $(p, v) \in V_{n+2}$, we have $(u, v) \in V_{n+2} \circ V_{n+2}$. 
By the given property of the sequence, $V_{n+2} \circ V_{n+2} \subseteq V_{n+1}$, so $(u, v) \in V_{n+1}$.
Since $V_{n+1}$ is symmetric, we also have $(v, u) \in V_{n+1}$.

Now, consider the element $v$. We know $v \in A_n(y)$. By the definition of $A_n(y)$, $A_n(y) \subseteq U_n(y)$. Thus $v \in U_n(y)$, which means $(y, v) \in U_n$.
We now have $(y, v) \in U_n$ and $(v, u) \in V_{n+1}$. By the definition of composite relation, this implies $(y, u) \in V_{n+1} \circ U_n$.
Recall that $U_n = V_n \circ V_{n-1} \circ \cdots \circ V_1$. Therefore,
$V_{n+1} \circ U_n = V_{n+1} \circ V_n \circ \cdots \circ V_1 = U_{n+1}$
This shows that $(y, u) \in U_{n+1}$, which means $u \in U_{n+1}(y)$.

However, we also know that $u \in A_n(x)$. By definition,
$A_n(x) = U_n(x) \setminus \bigcup_{z \prec x, z \neq x} U_{n+1}(z)$
Since $y \prec x$ and $y \neq x$, the set $U_{n+1}(y)$ is one of the sets in the union being subtracted. Therefore, for $u$ to be in $A_n(x)$, it must be that $u \notin U_{n+1}(y)$.

We have established both $u \in U_{n+1}(y)$ and $u \notin U_{n+1}(y)$, which is a contradiction. 

Thus, our initial assumption must be false. For any $p \in X$, the set $V_{n+2}(p)$ intersects at most one element of $\mathcal{A}_n$. This proves that $\mathcal{A}_n$ is a discrete set of subsets.
